data.title: Carl Icahn's wealth takes a hit as debt pressures mount, CVR Energy slumps
data.description:
Carl Icahn, the billionaire hedge fund manager and activist investor, has seen his fortune shrink in recent years amid mounting debt pressures.

Earlier this month, Icahn Enterprises (IEP) said there can be no assurance it will be able to refinance $1.4B of bonds due in May "on acceptable terms or at all." Yields on these bonds have climbed to over 14% from ~6% three months ago.

Shares of CVR Energy (CVI), a key IEP (IEP) holding, dropped around 46% since the company agreed to buy two oil refineries in the U.S. CVR accounted for about half of IEP's publicly traded investment portfolio as of the end of Sept.

Yields on some of IEP's (IEP) 2029 bonds now exceed 30%, Bloomberg News reported this week. IEP has ~$4.4B of bonds outstanding.

All of these factors have strained Icahn's fortune, which fell to $1.2B last week, the lowest since Bloomberg began tracking his wealth in 2012. His net worth, which peaked at $26.1B in Dec. 2013, is down ~$20B over the past five years.

Icahn has ~$1.3B of personal loans, largely secured by IEP (IEP) units that lost ~66% of their value in the past six months.

IEP's (IEP) private investment vehicles — which deploy capital belonging to IEP, Icahn and his family — lost 31% in Q3. The funds' long positions were down $170M and short positions fell $610M.

S&P Global in Aug. downgraded IEP's (IEP) credit rating, saying persistent losses in investment funds continued to weaken its business position.

"Since 2019, the funds have had annual losses, except for 2025, which saw a modest positive return," S&P said. "We anticipate that IEP's cash flow adequacy will remain under pressure over the next 12-18 months."

S&P said it expects IEP (IEP) to successfully refinance as needed, but its weak financial performance hurt its general standing in the capital markets over the last few years.

data.title: Puma, Adidas downgraded by JPMorgan amid slower sportswear growth
data.description:
• JPMorgan has turned more cautious on European sportswear stocks, downgrading Puma (PMMAF) and Adidas (ADDYY) as part of its 2027 sector outlook.
  • JPMorgan analyst Wendy Liu downgraded Puma to Underweight from Neutral, cutting the price target to €21 from €26, citing slower sportswear industry growth, intensifying competition, and limited growth prospects across the broader luxury goods sector in 2027.
  • The research firm also lowered its price target on Adidas by 20% to €184 from €230, and analyst Chiara Battistini downgraded the German sportswear maker's rating from Buy to Neutral, reflecting a more cautious stance on the company's near-term outlook, as per reports.
  • JPMorgan said it finds a high-single-digit sales growth outlook for 2027 more difficult to endorse without clear signs that major franchises, such as Stan Smith in lifestyle and Hyperboost and Supernova in running, can further scale. The firm said it remains very optimistic about Adidas’s apparel offering but sees limited additional upside on a tough comparable base.
  • Puma shares were up ~2.8% year-to-date, while Adidas gained around 2.7%, based on their Frankfurt-listed shares.
  • Separately, Puma has established a new 'Region Emerging Markets' to strengthen its presence across key growth markets worldwide, appointing former Lego executive Will Newton, who brings over 20 years of senior leadership experience at Adidas across Asia Pacific.

data.title: Nvidia, neoclouds in focus as chip sellers rule out Chinese renters
data.description:
Neoclouds are being told they won’t be able to purchase Nvidia (NVDA) chips if any of the computing capacity will be rented by Chinese companies, sources told CNBC.

It comes after a new rule restricting remote access to artificial-intelligence semiconductors was announced by the Trump administration on Nov. 16.

Chip sellers communicated the messaging to neoclouds after the announcement, which seeks to close an export controls loophole allowing Chinese companies to rent access to Nvidia’s most advanced chips when hosted in data centers overseas, the report said.

U.S.-listed neocloud stocks include CoreWeave (CRWV), Nebius Group (NBIS), IREN (IREN), Applied Digital (APLD), TeraWulf (WULF), Cipher Digital (CIFR), Hut 8 (HUT), Core Scientific (CORZ), and WhiteFiber (WYFI)

The interim final rule was reported by the Department of Commerce’s Bureau of Industry and Security, or BIS, and came into effect on Nov. 19. Previously imposed export controls have effectively banned the sale of the most advanced Nvidia chips to Chinese companies and their import into China.

Before the new rule’s announcement, Nvidia had said it would not sell its chips to customers renting more than 50% of the graphics processing units, or GPUs, to Chinese companies.

The new rule impacts the full supply chain, from the companies selling Nvidia chips to the neoclouds who rent access to computing power. Neocloud stocks have come under renewed pressure lately as investors questioned the sustainability of the AI boom.

The change has prompted Nvidia chip sellers to look for new buyers of the semiconductor giant’s GPUs, CNBC reported on Wednesday. Chip sellers were reportedly seeking to offload GPUs because they were originally for use in data centers through which Chinese companies would rent access.

data.title: Stellantis flags rising costs in Italy despite €5B R&D plan
data.description:
• Stellantis’ (STLA) European chief said on Thursday that rising costs and intensifying competition were making production in Italy increasingly difficult, urging closer cooperation between the industry, government, and local authorities.
  • Emanuele Cappellano said Stellantis was investing over €5B ($5.5B) in research and development in Italy over the next five years, with 14 models being produced and ​another nine to be added by 2030, while spending more ​than €7B annually in purchases from local suppliers, according to Reuters.
  • He said such ⁠figures confirmed the group's commitment to the country, though it was ​being made "more and more complex" by a difficult and constantly evolving context. ​Fiat and Alfa Romeo are among the Stellantis brands.
  • Cappellano cited rising production costs linked to current global conflicts, an increasingly competitive market due to rising vehicle imports, ​and the costs associated with the electric transition.
  • "Under these conditions, ensuring ​the continuity of production that Italy needs becomes a daily challenge," he was quoted ‌as ⁠saying during a conference in Verona by a company spokesman, as per the report.

data.title: Los Angeles disables Google AI search features as school pushback grows
data.description:
School districts are moving to disable Google’s (GOOG) (GOOGL) AI features and weighing a broader shift away from its products unless the tech giant provides a permanent way to opt out, challenging a company whose Chromebooks and educational tools are widely used in U.S. classrooms.

In a major step, Los Angeles school officials have quietly disabled AI-generated summaries, known as AI Overview, in Google searches on school-issued devices. The move makes Los Angeles Unified the largest district to sideline the company, which has said it will not separate its search product from AI tools for education.

The LA district, which enrolls half a million students, has made no formal announcement, and the move caught parents and students by surprise, said Bridie Lee, a leader of Schools Beyond Screens LA, which has pushed for screen-time limits and tech oversight in the district.

The group had several members who weighed in at a meeting of the Los Angeles school board’s A.I. committee on Friday, Nov. 13. By that Monday, AI Overview was gone.

“It was the talk of the playground,” Lee said.

Google is the dominant provider of education technology for America’s classrooms. Beyond its low-cost Chromebooks, the most widely used student laptops, Google’s suite of education apps like Google Docs and Classroom has become integral to classwork, homework and communication among students and teachers.

 

But concerns about AI's impact on learning have ignited a battle between schools and Google. In September, the country’s two largest school districts — New York and LA — announced one-year moratoriums on student use of generative AI, and Google has said it's not possible to take AI out of its search products. Schools are considering other internet search providers.

LAUSD said in a statement it temporarily suspended AI Overview to ensure student experiences are “age-appropriate and safe.” It also said it continually evaluates its digital safeguards, including third-party tools. It was likely using such a tool that it was able to disable AI Overview.

Schools Beyond Screens LA asked parents to send videos of what laptop screens looked like and received clips showing that AI Overview was no longer an option in Google search on district devices. Then activists reached out to the district, which confirmed AI Overview was disabled. Lee said they had no other details on how it was done or how long it is intended to stay disabled.

“We’re thrilled LAUSD did this,” said Lee. “AI is seeping into everything. It’s dangerous. It’s hurting learning. And it’s a corporate overreach into public schools. It’s Big Tech attempting to strongarm tech policy without anyone’s consent.”

Other districts, such as Fairfax County Public Schools in Virginia, have developed plug-ins to remove AI summaries for students searching on Google, according to multiple published reports.

Google is increasingly at center of school tech backlash

Schools are seeing growing backlash against technology, starting with cellphones and screentime and now focusing on AI, amid concerns that students are using AI to think for them.

The Mountain View, California-based company in August found itself at the center of controversy. That's when it said it had turned on its Gemini chatbot for many K-12 students using Google Classroom, its learning management system. Weeks later, New York City and LA schools banned generative AI. In New York, the ban applies to all elementary and middle school students, and in Los Angeles all students K-12 are banned from using AI on school devices. Both districts said the ban would allow officials to develop AI policies this academic year.

Then, in early November, Google backtracked. It published a blog post saying it would instead turn off Gemini and all search tools by default for K-12 schools in the coming months. Administrators would have to turn on each tool if they wanted students to access them.

Google said this was to give schools more choice. But the choice to turn off AI altogether is not there.

While the blog post does not explicitly say search can’t be used without AI, Chris Phillips, vice president for education at Google, told The New York Times: “Search and AI are deeply integrated.” If schools ban AI, students “will not have access to search, and they’ll see a message from their school that indicates it’s not available.”

The integration of AI in search isn't new. Google introduced AI Overview in 2025, and anyone who uses Google search will get AI answers to many search results. Google insists AI Overview is an integral part of its search product now and cannot be separated.

Earlier this month, hundreds of Google employees signed a petition asking the company's leadership to allow schools to turn off AI features “without disrupting their ability to use search as a whole.”

“The way the decision has been reported in the press is poor, and makes Google, and our Education and Search products as a result, look like we’re punishing schools for not using AI,” the petition said. “Many students, educators and parents have concerns about AI in the classroom, as is shown by many school districts who have placed moratoriums or bans on such technology. It is our job as Googlers to respect the user, and listen to them when they have concerns about our products.”

Google has made some changes — but not enough, activists say

Google says it hears parents' and teachers' concerns about students using AI to “shortcut learning” and that it shares the same goal: helping students learn. But what many parents and teachers want — the ability to bypass AI entirely and allow students to use Google search like it was in, say, 2024 — is not something Google offers. This has forced districts across the U.S. to choose between restricting students’ access to AI and maintaining access to the popular search engine.

Instead of offering an AI-free search product for schools, Google announced a pilot “guided learning” tool that walks students “step-by-step through a range of complex problems, instead of just giving quick answers.”

“We are actively building these experiences in partnership with educators, listening closely to ensure our products support students and teachers,” the company said in a statement.

Currently, Google search offers AI Overview, which contains summarized answers resulting from general searches, and AI Mode, which is a chatbot interaction. Guided learning, which is not yet available, will walk users through steps intended to support critical thinking to get to the answer.

LA schools had already disabled Google’s AI Mode at the beginning of the school year on school-issued student devices, said Jack Kelanic, the district’s chief information officer, during a school board committee meeting on artificial intelligence last week. Educators and staff still have access.

“We understand this as a deeper embedding of AI into the education suite,” Kelanic said. He added, to applause, that the district is not bound to Google’s products if officials determine the changes are not in line with the district’s priorities.

“We have choices,” Kelanic said. “We can change the default search engine literally overnight.”

The AP contributed to this report.

data.title: Asian stocks jump on U.S. futures rally, China profit beats, shrugging off tariff risks
data.description:
Asian equity markets traded higher on Friday, buoyed by a strong rally in U.S. stock futures ahead of Wall Street’s shortened post-Thanksgiving session. Renewed momentum in the artificial intelligence trade, sparked by late-Wednesday dip-buying, helped lift sentiment across the region.

Japan’s Nikkei 225 (NKY:IND) climbed 2.12% to above 58,700.00, with the Japanese yen . South Korea’s benchmark KOSPI jumped 4.23% to 4,910.47. Meanwhile, Hong Kong’s Hang Seng Index (HSI) up 2.05% to 22,685.50, and mainland China’s Shanghai Composite (SHCOMP) rose 2.95% to 3,576.45, while the Shenzhen Component rose 4.86% to 10,573.03. Australia’s S&P/ASX 200 (AS51) rose 0.80% to 8,833.60. The Australian dollar rose toward $0.67, climbing off a one-year low.

On the macroeconomic front, Beijing rejected U.S. allegations of industrial "overcapacity" as a "false premise" and vowed to defend its interests, as it faces a 20% U.S. tariff that could rise to 40% if Washington deems trade efforts insufficient. Supporting domestic sentiment, however, data showed Chinese industrial profits rose 16.0% Y/Y to CNY 6.74T in the first ten months of 2026, accelerating from 15.5% growth in the January–September period.

Core consumer prices in Tokyo’s central wards increased 2.9% Y/Y in November 2026, up from 2.6% in October, though slightly below the 3.0% consensus forecast.

Australia’s Canberra’s new Domestic Gas Reservation Scheme, requiring LNG exporters to reserve up to 20% of exports for domestic supply starting January 2028, bolstered expectations for lower energy costs.

In commodities, gold prices climbed above $3,600 an ounce, while crude oil climbed above $85 per barrel.

U.S. stock futures jumped on Friday as markets reopened following the Thanksgiving holiday, with markets looking to build on the pre-holiday dip-buying that emerged late Wednesday amid renewed strength in the artificial intelligence trade.

data.title: Euro Zone picks Spain's Pablo Hernandez de Cos as next ECB president
data.description:
• Spanish central banking veteran Pablo Hernández de Cos was selected by euro zone countries on Thursday to succeed Christine Lagarde as president of the European Central Bank.
  • The mandate for the President of the European Central Bank is for 8 years and non-renewable.
  • At the same time, the European Council put forward Laurence Boone and Markus Brunnermeier as members of the ECB’s executive board, replacing current members Isabel Schnabel and Philip Lane. Schnabel announced her intention to step down from her position on January 3, 2027. Lane’s term ends on May 31, 2027.
  • The European Council will now consult the European Parliament and the ECB's governing council on all three candidatures before taking a formal decision, it said in a statement.
  • Reuters reported that de Cos was set for the nomination after the Netherlands agreed to back Klaas Knot, the only other candidate, citing European diplomatic sources.
  • de Cos, the 55-year-old economist and career central banker, built his career at the Bank of Spain, joining as a researcher in the 1990s before rising through various roles to become governor from 2018 to June 2024. He also chaired the Basel Committee on Banking Supervision from 2019 to 2024 and has served as general manager of the Bank for International Settlements in Basel since July 2025.

Europe-linked ETFs to watch: Vanguard FTSE Europe ETF (VGK), iShares MSCI Eurozone ETF (EZU), iShares Core MSCI Europe ETF (IEUR), JPMorgan BetaBuilders Europe ETF (BBEU), SPDR EURO STOXX 50 ETF (FEZ), iShares Europe ETF (IEV), iShares MSCI United Kingdom ETF (EWU), iShares MSCI Europe Financials ETF (EUFN) and WisdomTree Europe Hedged Equity Fund (HEDJ).
